fixes.explanation: That number belongs to the first try at Ai. About three thousand men went up then, and they fled before the men of Ai (Joshua 7:4). This time the LORD tells Joshua, Israel's leader, “Take the whole army with you…” I once tried to carry a whole day's cookie boxes in one trip, and crumbs went everywhere. Israel isn't sent back with the same small crew.

The elders are in the story, but the order is bigger than that. Joshua, Israel's leader, is told to take the whole army. Later, Joshua and the elders of Israel march before the troops up to Ai (Joshua 8:10). So the elders walk out front, and the army is right behind them.

That's the plan for Jericho, not Ai. At Jericho the people marched around the city once a day and returned to camp for six days, and on the seventh day they went around it seven times (Joshua 6:14–15). Ai gets a different plan. The LORD tells Joshua, "Set up an ambush behind the city."

Yes. Joshua says the men of Ai will say, “The Israelites are running away from us as they did before.” Joshua is counting on what happened the first time to shape what they say this time. It's like when a friend has bailed on you twice, so the third time you say "he's bailing again" before you even check your phone. Joshua's plan has Israel flee so that Ai follows and gets drawn away from the city.

Supplies never come up. Joshua tells his men what he expects the men of Ai to say: “The Israelites are running away from us as they did before.” His words are about Israel running, like the first time. The camp's pantry isn't part of it. Joshua says this so his men know why Israel is going to flee on purpose.

Nothing in these verses says anything about Joshua being hurt. Joshua says the men of Ai will say, “The Israelites are running away from us as they did before.” His words are about Israel running like the first time. That's the picture he wants Ai to follow as they chase.

That's right. Joshua tells the men in ambush that as Israel flees, “…you are to rise from the ambush and seize the city…” He adds, “…for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand.” Later the LORD tells Joshua to hold out his battle lance toward Ai, and as soon as he does, the men in ambush rise quickly (Joshua 8:18–19). Good timing is half of any plan.

No searching in the orders. Joshua says, “…set it on fire.” That's the instruction for after the ambush has taken the city. When it happens, the men in ambush capture the city and immediately set it on fire (Joshua 8:19).

Yes, north. The troops “…camped to the north of it, with the valley between them and the city.” The ambush is placed in a different spot, to the west of the city. The text says the king of Ai did not know an ambush had been set up behind his city (Joshua 8:14).

Not quite. The king of Ai sees the Israelites and hurries out early in the morning to meet them in battle. But the text says “…he did not know that an ambush had been set up against him behind the city.” So the ambush stays hidden from him. That's why the plan works.

The Jordan is where Israel crossed into the land (Joshua 3), but it isn't where they run here. They “…fled toward the wilderness.” The men of Ai then follow them and are drawn away from the city. So the direction matters, because the wilderness leads Ai away from its own front door.

Not true. The text says, “Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel…” Every man went out, which means no men were left to guard the city. The text says the city was left “wide open while they pursued Israel.” That's the opening the ambush needs.

That's right. The text says, “Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel, leaving the city wide open while they pursued Israel.” Every man went out after Israel. There were no men left behind to guard the city. That's exactly the opening the men in ambush take.

Yes, smoke. “When the men of Ai turned and looked back, the smoke of the city was rising into the sky.” The men in ambush had rushed into the city, captured it and immediately set it on fire (Joshua 8:19). So when Ai looks back, the smoke is what they see. The text goes on to say they could not escape in any direction.

Not mist. The text says, “…the smoke of the city was rising into the sky.” The men of Ai turn and look back and see it. The fire was set by the men in ambush, who captured the city and immediately set it on fire (Joshua 8:19). Smoke is the word the writer uses.

That's right, it's False. The text says the men of Ai have no way out in any direction. Their city is burning behind them, and the troops who had fled to the wilderness turn on their pursuers. Then those in the ambush come out of the city, and the men of Ai are trapped between the Israelite forces on both sides (Joshua 8:22).

Yes. “But they took the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua.” The men of Ai who pursued Israel were struck down until no survivor or fugitive remained (Joshua 8:22). The king is the one taken alive instead. Joshua deals with him later in the passage.

That's right. “Israel took for themselves only the cattle and plunder of that city, as the LORD had commanded Joshua.” At the start, the LORD told Joshua they could carry off the plunder and livestock for themselves (Joshua 8:2). So Israel takes what the LORD allowed and does it as He commanded. Nothing more is taken.

Yes. The text says “…over it they raised a large pile of rocks, which remains to this day.” That's after the body was taken down at sunset and thrown down at the entrance of the city gate. It's a heavy ending for a heavy passage, and the text tells it plainly. The rocks are still there when the writer tells it.
